title: Sleeping in the temple of Asclepius

confidence.note: The god's arrival in Athens in 420 BCE is recorded on a contemporary inscription, and the Epidaurus cure stelae are 4th-century BCE stones that survive. What they document is the practice and the sanctuary's claims, not the cures themselves.

summary: Greek patients slept in Asclepius's sanctuary hoping the god would heal them in a dream, and the priests carved the miracles in stone.
body: A sick Greek who had run out of remedies could take the case to a god. At sanctuaries of Asclepius, above all at Epidaurus in the Peloponnese, pilgrims slept in a hall called the abaton, hoping the god would appear in a dream. The sanctuary advertised its successes in stone. Four 4th-century BCE stelae, probably displayed in the incubation hall itself, carry about seventy cure stories: a man with an empty eye socket whose eyelids the god filled with a drug, a woman said to have been pregnant for five years, and a scoffer told to dedicate a silver pig "as a memorial of her ignorance."

This was no fringe cult. An inscription records the god's formal introduction to Athens in 420 BCE. It coexisted with the new naturalistic medicine: Plato could call Hippocrates himself "the Asclepiad," a member of the healing clan claiming descent from the god, and the Hippocratic Oath opens by swearing by Apollo and Asclepius.

Asclepius's emblem was a staff with a single snake. The winged, two-snaked caduceus belonged to Hermes, god of messengers and commerce; its modern medical use owes much to the US Army Medical Corps, which adopted it in 1902 through a misunderstanding.

myth.tradition: The caduceus, a winged staff with two snakes, is the ancient symbol of medicine.
myth.record: Asclepius carried a staff with one snake. The caduceus was Hermes's herald's wand; the US Army Medical Corps made it a medical badge in 1902 by mistake.

links.note: Hippocrates was called an Asclepiad; temple and naturalistic medicine coexisted.

title: Alcmaeon puts the mind in the brain

confidence.note: His book is lost and his dates are argued from later reports; scholars place it anywhere from c. 500 to after 470 BCE. His views on the brain survive through Theophrastus and other later writers, while the claim that he dissected rests on a misread passage.

people: Alcmaeon of Croton (active c. 500–450 BCE), natural philosopher and medical writer
summary: Around 500 BCE a thinker in southern Italy argued that we perceive and understand with the brain, not the heart.
body: Alcmaeon of Croton, in southern Italy, wrote a single book, probably between 500 and 450 BCE, that survives only in fragments and later reports. Later reports, chiefly from Theophrastus, make him the first to argue that the brain is the central organ of sensation and thought, linked by channels to the eyes and other sense organs. He also defined health as the "equality" of opposing powers in the body and disease as the "monarchy" of one. Often hailed as the first dissector, he may have done no more than cut out an animal's eye.

myth.tradition: Alcmaeon was the father of anatomy, dissecting bodies to trace the optic nerve to the brain.
myth.record: The later report praising his work on the eye mostly describes Herophilus' discoveries. At most he excised an animal's eyeball; there is no evidence of systematic dissection.

links.note: Herophilus' dissections revived Alcmaeon's view that the brain is the seat of sensation and intellect.

title: Hippocrates and the Hippocratic Corpus

date.display: Active late 5th century BCE (traditionally c. 460–370 BCE)

confidence.note: Plato's mentions confirm that Hippocrates was a well-known physician in his own lifetime, but his birth and death dates come from brief biographies written centuries later. The corpus survives and is dated on internal evidence to c. 430–350 BCE; which treatises, if any, he wrote himself is unresolved.

people: Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460–c. 370 BCE), physician and teacher
summary: The most famous name in Western medicine belongs to a man we barely know, attached to some sixty texts written by many hands.
body: Hippocrates of Cos is the most famous name in Western medicine and one of the most elusive. He was certainly real and renowned in his own time: in Plato's *Protagoras*, Socrates speaks of paying fees to "Hippocrates of Cos, the Asclepiad" to learn medicine. Beyond that, only the barest outline survives. Brief Lives written centuries later have him born on Cos around 460 BCE and dying at an advanced age at Larissa in Thessaly, and his career peaked during the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE).

Under his name survives the Hippocratic Corpus, about sixty works on diagnosis, epidemics, women's diseases, surgery, diet and more. Most date from the last decades of the 5th century and the first half of the 4th century BCE, and they were probably gathered together in Alexandria. They are the work of many authors and sometimes give contradictory advice. Even in antiquity scholars disagreed about which were genuine; modern scholars have no sample of his own prose against which to test them.

What unites much of the collection is an insistence that disease is natural. The author of *On the Sacred Disease* argues that epilepsy is no more divine than any other illness: "Men regard its nature and cause as divine from ignorance and wonder." Hippocratic doctors watched the patient, the season and the course of the illness, and treated mainly with diet, drugs and regimen. *Epidemics* I sums up the method: "Declare the past, diagnose the present, foretell the future."

Natural did not mean correct. The physiology was speculative. Each later age also rebuilt Hippocrates in its own image, as a chemist, a mechanist, a vitalist, a holist, even a patron of homeopathy. The Oath and the four humours both travel under his name, but the name is better read as the label of a tradition than as a signature.

myth.tradition: Hippocrates, the father of medicine, wrote the Hippocratic writings and single-handedly turned medicine from the gods to nature.
myth.record: About sixty texts by many authors over several generations travel under his name, and none can be securely assigned to him. Natural explanations of disease were shared by other thinkers, such as Alcmaeon, before and around him.

title: The Hippocratic Oath

confidence.note: The text survives, so what it says is certain, but who wrote it, when, and who actually swore it are unknown. It is usually placed in the 5th or 4th century BCE, possibly among the earlier Hippocratic texts; Jones notes that the ancient scholar Erotian accepted it as genuinely Hippocratic.

summary: The most famous oath in medicine bans poison and the knife, swears by Apollo, and never says "First, do no harm."
body: The Oath is the best-known text in the Hippocratic Corpus and one of the least understood. The swearer calls on Apollo the physician, Asclepius, Hygieia and Panacea, promises to treat his teacher like a parent, and then lists rules of conduct: use regimen for the patients' benefit and "do no harm or injustice to them"; give no lethal drug even if asked; give no woman a pessary to cause abortion; leave cutting for stone to those trained in it; commit no sexual misconduct in patients' homes, with free people or slaves; keep secret what is seen and heard.

Who wrote it, when and for whom is unknown. Its translator W. H. S. Jones admitted in 1923 that its relationship to the history of medicine was, "in our present state of knowledge, unknowable," and wondered whether it was ever a reality or merely a "counsel of perfection." Its family-like obligations may mark the moment when the Asclepiads of Cos began teaching outsiders.
The most quoted line is not in it. "First, do no harm" appears nowhere in the Oath; the nearest Hippocratic phrase is in *Epidemics* I: "to help, or at least to do no harm."

myth.tradition: Every doctor swears the Hippocratic Oath, which begins "First, do no harm."
myth.record: The phrase is not in the Oath; a similar maxim appears in Epidemics I. Most modern medical schools do not require the original Oath, and some use rewritten versions.

title: The four humours

confidence.note: *On the Nature of Man* survives and is dated on internal evidence to the late 5th or early 4th century BCE; Aristotle's citation supports Polybus as at least part-author. The theory's long dominance is abundantly documented, though when it finally lost its grip varies by place and by field.

people: Polybus (late 5th century BCE), pupil and son-in-law of Hippocrates, probable author of *On the Nature of Man*
Galen of Pergamon (129–216 CE), who systematized humoral medicine
summary: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile: a theory set out in one Greek treatise ran Western medicine for some two thousand years.
body: For roughly two thousand years, learned Western physicians explained health and illness through four fluids. The classic statement is in *On the Nature of Man*, a treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus: "The body of man has in itself blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile; these make up the nature of his body." A person was healthiest when the four were properly proportioned and mixed; pain followed when one was in excess or deficit, or separated from the rest.

The author was probably not Hippocrates. Aristotle quoted a passage of the treatise as the work of Polybus, Hippocrates' pupil and son-in-law, though an ancient medical papyrus, the *Anonymus Londinensis*, credits one passage to Polybus and another to Hippocrates himself. Nor was the scheme the only one on offer: some Hippocratic writers counted water, blood, phlegm and bile instead. In the end black bile displaced water.

The theory was reasonable on the evidence of the time. Blood and phlegm were obvious, yellow bile showed in jaundice and in the gall bladders of animals, and black bile seemed to explain conditions that darkened the skin. Galen tied the humours to the qualities hot, cold, wet and dry and to Aristotle's four elements, so that the body mirrored the cosmos and each person had a temperament, such as sanguine. Therapy followed logically: remove an excess by bleeding, purging, vomiting or sweating, adjust diet and habits, and treat a hot illness with a cold remedy.

Through Galen and the Arabic writers, above all Ibn Sina, the system governed medieval and Renaissance medicine, and it still lives on in traditional Arabic medicine. In Europe the new sciences of the 17th century undermined its foundations, yet bleeding and purging persisted through the 18th century, and only the bacteriological revolution of the late 19th century drove the humours out of orthodox medicine.

myth.tradition: Hippocrates devised the theory of the four humours.
myth.record: The canonical four appear in one treatise, *On the Nature of Man*, which ancient testimony attributes largely to Polybus; other Hippocratic texts used different fluids, and Galen made the scheme canonical.

title: The Plague of Athens

confidence.note: Thucydides, who caught the disease and survived, dates it to the second year of the war. That it happened is beyond doubt; what it was is not, and a 2006 claim of typhoid DNA was promptly disputed.

people: Thucydides, Athenian historian and general who survived the disease
summary: An epidemic killed perhaps a third of wartime Athens; the historian who described it survived, but nobody knows what the disease was.
body: In 430 BCE, in the second year of the war with Sparta, an epidemic struck crowded wartime Athens, killing by one modern estimate as much as a third of the population. Thucydides, who caught it and survived, described sudden fever, inflamed eyes and a bloody throat, and noted that doctors died fastest because they saw the sick most. What it was remains unknown: modern writers have proposed at least 29 diseases, from smallpox to Ebola. In 2006 a team reported typhoid DNA in teeth from a mass grave of at least 150 people, but other geneticists replied that this was "no proof."

myth.tradition: Ancient DNA has shown that the Plague of Athens was typhoid fever.
myth.record: A 2006 study reported Salmonella Typhi sequences from victims' teeth, but the result was immediately challenged and is not accepted as proof.

links.note: Asclepius was brought to Athens a decade later.

title: Human dissection at Alexandria

confidence.note: That Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies is accepted on the strength of their findings as reported by Galen and others, though all their own books are lost and their exact dates are uncertain. The charge of human vivisection rests on Celsus and later Christian writers, and scholars remain divided over it.

people: Herophilus of Chalcedon (born late 4th century BCE), anatomist who taught under Ptolemy I and II
Erasistratus of Ceos (born c. 304 BCE), anatomist and physiologist
summary: For a few decades, Greek doctors in Ptolemaic Alexandria cut open human bodies, and were later accused of cutting open living criminals too.
body: For a few decades in the early 3rd century BCE, in the new Greek capital of Egypt, physicians did something almost no one else in the ancient world would do: they systematically dissected human bodies. Two names are attached to the work. Herophilus of Chalcedon taught at Alexandria under the first two Ptolemies; Erasistratus of Ceos was his younger contemporary. Elsewhere in the Greek world cutting up a human corpse was abhorrent. In Alexandria it was not, perhaps partly because Egyptian embalming made opening the body familiar.

The results were remarkable. Herophilus distinguished the cerebrum from the cerebellum, traced the nerves from the brain and spinal cord, followed the paths from the eyes to the brain, and named the duodenum; the meeting point of the brain's venous sinuses is still called the *torcular Herophili*. He studied the pulse, by one late report timing it with a water clock. Erasistratus described the brain's cavities and membranes and agreed that the nerves start in the brain. None of their books survive; we know their work mainly through Galen.

The darkest question is whether they also opened the living. The Roman encyclopedist Celsus, writing in the 1st century CE, reported that some physicians praised Herophilus and Erasistratus for laying open "men whilst alive — criminals received out of prison from the kings." Celsus himself called the practice "as cruel as it is needless." The Christian writer Tertullian later called Herophilus a "butcher" who "cut up no end of persons." Galen says nothing of it, and scholars are still divided over whether the charge is history or polemic.

The window soon closed. By Galen's time, in the 2nd century CE, human dissection was no longer culturally possible. He dissected apes, pigs and other animals, and advised students to seize any chance to see a human skeleton or, better, to visit Alexandria, the only place where training still used one. His ape-based anatomy stood until Vesalius published the *Fabrica* in 1543. Systematic dissection of human bodies did not become an accepted way of learning again for many centuries.

myth.tradition: The Alexandrian anatomists routinely vivisected condemned criminals handed over by the king.
myth.record: The story comes from Celsus, writing some three centuries later, and from Christian polemicists such as Tertullian. Galen is silent, and historians remain divided over whether it is true.

title: Mithridatium and theriac

confidence.note: The antidote is known only from Roman writers of the following century, whose recipes disagree completely; the king's immunity to poison is a legend. Its later career as theriac is well attested.

people: Pompey (Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus), Roman general who defeated him
Andromachus, physician to the emperor Nero
summary: A poison-proof king, a recipe found in his private papers, and an antidote whose descendants were still trusted in the 18th century.
body: Mithridates VI of Pontus, the most powerful king of his day, was said to have protected himself by taking poison daily, and his name stuck to a famous antidote. No one agreed what was in it. Pliny says Pompey found the king's own recipe after defeating him: two dried walnuts, two figs, twenty rue leaves and a grain of salt. Celsus's version of "the most famous antidote" has some three dozen ingredients taken up in honey. A similar compound credited to Andromachus, Nero's physician, became theriac, a remedy still trusted in the 18th century; English "treacle" comes from its name.

myth.tradition: Mithridates made himself immune to every poison with a secret universal antidote.
myth.record: The story is told by Roman writers a century later, whose recipes range from four ingredients to three dozen; Pliny's 19th-century translators called the immunity "a mere fable."

title: Celsus, De Medicina

confidence.note: Celsus is placed under Tiberius by references in Quintilian, Pliny and Columella, but nothing else of his life is known, and whether he was a practicing doctor is disputed. The text itself survives, and its printing in Florence in 1478 is documented.

people: Aulus Cornelius Celsus (active c. 25 CE), Roman encyclopedist
summary: A Roman encyclopedia's medical books, written in elegant Latin, gave medicine its classic four signs of inflammation.
body: Aulus Cornelius Celsus compiled a Latin encyclopedia in Rome under the emperor Tiberius; its eight medical books made his name. Whether he practiced medicine himself is still argued. *De Medicina* surveys the Greek medical schools, diet, drugs and surgery in clear, elegant prose, and gives the classic definition: "the signs of an inflammation are four: redness and swelling with heat and pain." Copied in the 15th century from a very old manuscript since lost, it was printed at Florence in 1478, among the first medical books to reach print, and ran to 49 editions by 1841.
